claims.text: Applying HPHT treatment during melt processing of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Applying HPHT treatment increases the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Conventional rapid quenching of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys typically produces only a limited amorphous region with moderate thermal stability.
The intervention uses pressures of several GPa and elevated temperature immediately before rapid quenching.
The intervention temperature should be above the alloy liquidus.
HPHT promotes a more uniform, hierarchically patterned atomic arrangement.
HPHT enhances atomic mixing and reduces local compositional fluctuations.
The more uniform atomic arrangement suppresses early nucleation of crystalline phases.
Applying high pressure and temperature reduces atomic mobility during cooling.
Applying high pressure and temperature increases atomic-packing homogeneity.
Reduced mobility and greater packing homogeneity delay nucleation kinetics.
Delayed nucleation promotes retention of the amorphous state and increases resistance to crystallization during subsequent heating.
HPHT-treated alloys will have a higher critical casting thickness for obtaining a fully amorphous state than conventionally quenched controls.
HPHT-treated alloys will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than conventionally quenched controls.
The beneficial effect requires a cooling rate high enough to preserve the HPHT-induced disordered state.
The intervention may be less effective when the alloy has insufficient atomic-size mismatch or mixing entropy to favor amorphization.
The intervention may fail when pressure, temperature, or duration lies outside an optimal range.
A treatment of approximately 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours is a proposed HPHT test condition.
